sat.title: How This Test Actually Works
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome to SAT Notes, episode one. I'm Lehua. Today we answer the question nobody asks out loud. What even is this test? Derek is here, Coach Pono is here, and Kaden is here with a breakfast burrito.
KADEN: It's a second breakfast. First one was at home.
DEREK: Two breakfasts. Bold.
LEHUA: Okay, Kaden, what do you think the SAT is right now? Be honest.
KADEN: Honestly? A four-hour paper test with a lot of reading and one kid sharpening his pencil the whole time.
DEREK: That was true a long time ago. It is not true now. Let me lay it out.
DEREK: The SAT is digital. You take it on a laptop or tablet in an app called Bluebook. It has two sections. Reading and Writing comes first, then Math.
DEREK: Each section is split into two modules. A Reading and Writing module is twenty-seven questions in thirty-two minutes. A Math module is twenty-two questions in thirty-five minutes. So the whole test is two hours and fourteen minutes of testing, with one ten-minute break between the two sections.
KADEN: Wait, that's it? That's like one long movie with all the trailers.
LEHUA: About that, yeah. Way shorter than the old paper test. And most people don't know that.
PONO: Okay, now the part that makes everybody nervous. The test is adaptive. Listen, dis one is important.
PONO: Module one is a mix of easy, medium, and hard questions. Everybody gets a module like that. How you do on module one decides your module two. Do well, and module two is the harder version. Do less well, and module two is the easier version.
KADEN: So if I get the hard one, that means I'm doing bad?
PONO: The opposite. The harder module two is the one that can give you the higher score. If module two feels tough, that is usually good news.
PONO: It's like a rodeo draw. Ride your first horse clean, and they give you the horse that scores big points. The rough horse is the prize.
KADEN: I don't want the rough horse.
PONO: You want the rough horse. Trust me.
LEHUA: And this is why we keep saying module one matters. Each module has its own clock, so rushing module one doesn't save you any time for later. It just costs you accuracy.
DEREK: One more detail. A few questions in each module are unscored. College Board is testing them for future tests. You can't tell which ones they are, so treat every question as if it counts.
KADEN: Okay, scoring. What's a good score? Like, what's the number.
DEREK: Each section is scored from two hundred to eight hundred. Add them together and the total runs from four hundred to sixteen hundred.
DEREK: For context, the national average total for the class of twenty twenty-five was one thousand twenty-nine. That's from College Board's own report.
KADEN: So anything over that is good?
DEREK: Anything over that is above average. Whether it's good depends on where you're applying.
LEHUA: Right, and this is the part I want Big Island kids to hear. A good score is not one number. It's a number compared to the schools on your list.
DEREK: Most colleges publish a middle fifty percent range for their admitted or enrolled students. That means a quarter of those students scored below the low number, and a quarter scored above the high number. You can find it on the school's admissions page, or on College Board's BigFuture site.
DEREK: So the rule is this. If your score is inside that range, you're a normal applicant there. If it's at or above the top of the range, your score helps you. If it's below the bottom, think hard about whether to send it.
KADEN: What about UH? Most of my friends are going to UH.
DEREK: Good question. As of this fall, the flagship UH campus is test-optional. You choose whether to send a score. And they have what they call a "Do No Harm" policy. If a score you send would hurt your chances for admission or a scholarship, they leave it out.
KADEN: Wait, so there's no downside to sending it?
DEREK: For admission there, by their own policy, no. And some scholarships and some direct-entry programs may want a score, so a good score can still mean money. Check the admissions page for your year, because policies change.
LEHUA: What about mainland schools? Mainland public universities and private colleges.
DEREK: A lot of mainland public universities are test-optional too, and a strong score can still help with merit scholarships. Several highly selective private colleges have gone back to requiring scores in recent years. So the honest answer is, look up every school on your list, every year. Don't trust what your cousin heard two years ago.
PONO: Your cousin also said the North Shore was flat in December.
KADEN: My cousin lies a lot.
LEHUA: Okay, Derek, give him the one rule that changes how he takes the whole test.
DEREK: There is no guessing penalty. A wrong answer and a blank answer both earn zero points. So a blank can never help you. Answer every question.
KADEN: Every question? Even if I have no idea?
DEREK: Every question. We have a whole episode on making those guesses smarter by crossing out wrong answers. That's episode two.
LEHUA: Let's do a little tour of the actual test, because the tools are built in. Derek, Math first.
DEREK: In Math, about three quarters of the questions are multiple choice. The other quarter, you type in your own answer. That's called a student-produced response. And there's a Desmos graphing calculator built right into Bluebook. You can also bring an approved calculator of your own.
KADEN: Desmos is in there? That's kind of a cheat code.
DEREK: It's a tool, not a cheat code. Use it to graph and check, not to avoid learning the algebra. There's also a reference sheet with the main geometry formulas, and we'll go through what's on it in episode eleven.
LEHUA: And Reading and Writing?
PONO: Reading and Writing uses short passages. One short passage, one question. You are not reading a five-page story and answering ten questions about it. You read a paragraph, you answer one thing, and you move on.
KADEN: Okay, that's way less scary.
PONO: Way less. And every question has a flag to mark it for review, and a tool to cross out choices. And at the bottom there's a grid that shows every question and which ones you answered. That's your dashboard. Like the gauges on your truck.
KADEN: I don't have a truck. I have a bus pass.
PONO: Then it's like the bus schedule. You check it, you don't stare at it.
LEHUA: So let's recap the facts, then homework. Kaden, you do it.
KADEN: Okay. Digital, on Bluebook. Two sections, Reading and Writing, then Math. Two modules each. Twenty-seven questions in thirty-two minutes for Reading and Writing, twenty-two in thirty-five for Math. Module one decides module two, and the hard module two is good news. Scores from four hundred to sixteen hundred. No guessing penalty. Never leave a blank.
DEREK: That's a clean summary.
KADEN: Rate it.
DEREK: Eight.
KADEN: I'll take it.
LEHUA: Homework. Open the app. Take the placement check if you haven't. It's two questions per skill, and it tells the dashboard where to start you. Then tap the official practice button and look at Bluebook. You don't have to take a full test yet. Just open it, so it isn't a stranger on test day.
PONO: Know the place before you get there.
LEHUA: That's episode one. Episode two is crossing out, how to find the wrong answers. Thanks for listening, everybody.
KADEN: Can I finish my burrito now?
LEHUA: Finish your burrito.

choices: Two sections, Reading and Writing then Math, each split into two modules

choices: You did well on Module 1 and unlocked the module that can score higher

sat.title: Crossing Out: How to Find the Wrong Answers
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode two. I'm Lehua. Sarah is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here with a hoodie over his whole face.
KADEN: It's cold in here. I'm conserving heat.
SARAH: It's a recording booth, not a freezer.
LEHUA: Okay, Kaden, warm-up question from last time. What's the one rule about blanks on the SAT?
KADEN: No blanks. A wrong answer and a blank both get zero, so a blank can never help you. Answer everything.
DEREK: Correct. No guessing penalty.
LEHUA: Good. So if you have to answer everything, the next question is obvious. How do you answer well when you don't know? That's today. Crossing out.
SARAH: And I want to say this right away. Crossing out is not a backup plan for when you're lost. It's how good test takers find the right answer on purpose. You don't hunt for the right answer first. You hunt for the wrong ones, because wrong answers have fingerprints.
KADEN: Fingerprints?
SARAH: Patterns. The test writers build wrong answers on purpose, and they build them the same few ways every time. Once you know the patterns, you start seeing them everywhere.
DEREK: Let me do the math part first, because it's short. Every SAT multiple-choice question has four choices. A blind guess is one in four. Cross out one choice you can prove is wrong, and you're at one in three. Cross out two, and it's a coin flip. Cross out three, and you didn't guess at all. You solved it backward.
KADEN: Okay, that's actually kind of fire. Like a boss fight where you take out the minions first and the boss is just standing there alone.
LEHUA: There it is.
DEREK: And Bluebook has a tool for this built in. You can strike out choices right on the screen. The app has the same thing, a little x next to every choice.
SARAH: One rule with the x. Only cross out a choice when you can say why it's wrong. Out loud in your head, one sentence. If you can't say why, leave it standing.
KADEN: What happens if I cross out the right one by accident?
SARAH: The app will tell you. If you miss a question and you had crossed out the right answer, it says so. That's a sign you were tapping the x on a feeling, not a reason.
LEHUA: So, Sarah, the fingerprints. What are they?
SARAH: The app gives every wrong answer a name when you miss it. It shows up as a little label, like "Trap: opposite." There are ten names in the app. Today we'll use the six you meet most in Reading and Writing, because those are the ones you can spot while you read.
SARAH: One. Too extreme. The choice says always, never, completely, or proves, when the passage only says some or might.
SARAH: Two. Half right. The first half of the choice matches the passage, and the second half goes wrong.
SARAH: Three. True but irrelevant. The choice is a real detail from the passage, but it doesn't answer this question.
SARAH: Four. Opposite. The choice flips what the passage says. It uses the right topic, but points the wrong direction.
SARAH: Five. Adds an assumption. The choice needs one extra idea the passage never gave you.
SARAH: Six. Near miss. Mostly grammar. It looks almost right but has one small error, like a comma in the wrong place.
KADEN: That's a lot of names.
LEHUA: You don't have to memorize them today. When you miss one in the app, read the label. After a week, you'll know them the way you know your friends' ringtones.
SARAH: Let's do one. This is a Words in Context question. When I say "blank," that's the missing word. I'll read it twice. Kaden, just listen.
SARAH: "The coach was usually blunt, but after the loss she was unusually blank, choosing every word carefully so no player felt singled out." Which word fits the blank? A, blunt. B, diplomatic. C, timid. D, talkative.
SARAH: One more time. "The coach was usually blunt, but after the loss she was unusually blank, choosing every word carefully so no player felt singled out." A, blunt. B, diplomatic. C, timid. D, talkative.
LEHUA: Everybody listening, pause it and try. Cross out what you can, and say why.
LEHUA: Okay, we're back. Kaden, go.
KADEN: I want to say timid. Because she's being careful.
SARAH: Good, you're thinking, so let's walk it the slow way. Start with the clues. The sentence says usually blunt, but. That word "but" means the blank is going to be different from blunt. So which choice can we cross out first?
KADEN: A. Blunt. It's literally the word she's not being.
SARAH: Right. And that's the trap we're naming today. Opposite. The sentence flips away from blunt, and choice A flips it right back. Opposite answers love to borrow a word straight from the passage, because it feels familiar.
SARAH: Next clue. "Choosing every word carefully so no player felt singled out." That's about how she talks to people. Which choice has nothing to do with that?
KADEN: D. Talkative. Nothing says she talked a lot.
SARAH: Cross it out. Now it's timid against diplomatic. And this is where it gets good. Timid has the right idea. She is being careful. But timid means scared or shy. Does the sentence say she's scared?
KADEN: No. It says she's careful so nobody feels bad.
SARAH: So timid is right idea, wrong word. It's close in feeling but wrong in meaning. Diplomatic means careful with words so you don't hurt people. That matches every clue. The answer is B.
KADEN: Okay, so I was close.
DEREK: Close is how they get you. The test writers want you to stop at the first choice that feels okay.
SARAH: Here's the habit. Before you pick, cross out until you have a reason for every x. If you get down to two and they both feel fine, put each one into the sentence and read it again. The wrong one usually sounds off in one specific spot.
LEHUA: And what if you get down to two and still can't decide?
DEREK: Then you pick one and move on. You have a fifty-fifty shot, which is twice as good as a blind guess. Flag it if you want to come back. Don't burn two minutes on it.
LEHUA: My auntie posted "let's eat grandma" on her page last week. No comma. I screenshotted it for you, Sarah.
SARAH: I saw it. I commented with the comma. She did not ask.
KADEN: Did she reply?
SARAH: She deleted my comment. Worth it.
LEHUA: Okay, bring it home. Kaden, recap. In your own words.
KADEN: Okay. Don't hunt for the right answer first. Hunt for the wrong ones. Every cross-out makes a guess better, four to three to two. Only cross out when I can say why it's wrong. The app names the traps, like too extreme, half right, true but irrelevant, opposite, adds an assumption, and near miss. Today's trap was opposite, where the choice flips what the passage says, and it usually steals a word from the passage. And if I'm down to two, plug both in, pick one, and move on.
LEHUA: Derek?
DEREK: That was organized. You got all six names in order. Nine.
KADEN: Nine? What's a ten?
DEREK: Nobody knows.
LEHUA: Homework. Open the app and go to Drill. Pick Reading and Writing, the whole section. Use the x on every question, even the easy ones, and make yourself say why before you tap it. When you miss one, read the trap label. Get used to the names.
SARAH: And if you see "Trap: opposite," go back and find the word in the sentence that flipped it.
LEHUA: That's episode two. Next time is episode three, the time squeeze. Thanks for listening, everybody.
KADEN: Can I take the hoodie off now?
SARAH: You could have taken it off twenty minutes ago.

sat.title: The Time Squeeze
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode three. I'm Lehua. Today is the one everybody asks about. The clock. Coach Pono is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here looking like he already ran out of time.
KADEN: I was up late. My alarm was early. It's a whole thing.
PONO: Kaden, that's the episode. You ran out of time before the test started. Welcome.
LEHUA: Warm-up from last time first. Kaden, when are you allowed to cross out a choice?
KADEN: Only when I can say why it's wrong. If I cross out the right one, the app calls me out.
LEHUA: Good. Hold on to that, it comes back today.
LEHUA: So, Coach, set it up. Why does the clock feel like it's attacking people?
PONO: Because they treat it like a bull. They fight it. You cannot fight a clock. The clock is a horse. You don't beat a horse, you ride it. You set a pace, you check it twice, and you don't let it decide where you're going.
DEREK: I'm going to say the actual numbers now, because Coach is going to keep saying horse.
PONO: I'm gonna keep saying horse.
DEREK: Reading and Writing. Two modules. Each one is twenty-seven questions in thirty-two minutes. That's about seventy-one seconds a question. Math. Two modules. Twenty-two questions in thirty-five minutes. About ninety-five seconds a question.
KADEN: Seventy-one seconds is nothing.
DEREK: Seventy-one seconds is plenty if you don't spend four minutes on question nine.
LEHUA: And that's the real problem, right? Nobody runs out of time evenly. They run out because of two or three questions that ate everything.
PONO: Exactly. The clock didn't beat you. One question beat you, and then the clock just told you about it.
KADEN: Okay so what do I actually do.
PONO: Two passes. First pass, you ride through in order. You look at a question. If you can see the path in about ten seconds, you take it. If you can't see the path, you pick your best guess, you flag it, and you move on. You do not sit there. Sitting there is fighting the horse.
KADEN: But what if I almost have it.
DEREK: "Almost have it" is the most expensive phrase on the SAT. Three more minutes on that one question is two or three questions you never reach. Those could be easy. The one you're stuck on, by definition, is not.
LEHUA: And when you guess, cross out first, like last episode.
DEREK: Right. Every choice you can prove wrong makes the guess better. One in four becomes one in three, then a coin flip. Small moves, real points.
LEHUA: Say the guessing rule, Derek, because people still don't believe it.
DEREK: There is no guessing penalty. None. On the SAT and on the ACT. A blank is a guaranteed zero. A guess at least has a chance. So a blank is the only answer that is always wrong.
KADEN: So I should just guess on everything?
DEREK: You should answer everything. Guessing is what you do when you've run out of better options. But the rule is, no blanks. Ever. Done.
PONO: Second pass. If you have time left, go back to the flags. You already have an answer on every one of them, so you're not rescuing anything, you're just upgrading. Start with the one that looked closest. Leave the monster for last. If the clock runs out while you're on the monster, who cares, you already answered it.
LEHUA: And on the digital SAT the flag is built in. There's a button. And there's a little grid at the bottom that shows you every question and whether you answered it. Use the grid. That's your dashboard.
KADEN: What about checkpoints? My tutor said something about checkpoints.
PONO: Your tutor's right. You look at the clock exactly twice. Not every thirty seconds. Twice. At the one-third mark and the two-thirds mark. And you ask one question. Am I at or past the target?
DEREK: Reading and Writing, that's question nine at ten minutes forty, and question eighteen at twenty-one minutes twenty. Math, question seven at eleven forty, and question fifteen at twenty-three twenty. Those are minutes used. The Bluebook clock counts down, so do that subtraction once before test day, not during it. The targets are in the app on the Time Squeeze page, you don't have to memorize them right now.
PONO: If you're behind, you flag faster. That's it. You don't panic, you don't speed-read, you just lower the bar for what you'll flag. If you're ahead, you slow down one notch.
KADEN: Being ahead is bad?
PONO: Ahead is fine. Ahead and careless is the problem. So use the extra time to read every word.
LEHUA: Let's talk about what happens in the last sixty seconds, because that's where people lose points they already had.
DEREK: In the last minute, you stop solving. Full stop. You open the grid, you look for anything unanswered, and you put something in. Then you stop. A half-finished solution is worth zero. A guess is worth something.
KADEN: What if I'm in the middle of a question and I have it?
DEREK: If you have it, you have it. Finish it, then check the grid. But "I have it" means you're writing the answer, not "I think I see where this goes."
LEHUA: Okay, Kaden, you're the one who actually takes this thing. What goes wrong for you?
KADEN: Honestly? Reading. I get into a passage and I read the whole thing like it's a book. Then the question is about one sentence and I'm like, I don't remember that sentence.
LEHUA: Yeah, that's the number one time leak in Reading and Writing. The digital SAT gives you one short passage per question. One. It's not a long passage with ten questions. So the move is, read the question first, then read the passage knowing what you're hunting for. That gets a whole episode of its own, episode five.
DEREK: Math version. Read the last sentence of the word problem first. That's the actual question. Then read the rest to collect the numbers. You'll stop doing arithmetic you didn't need.
KADEN: Okay that one's actually good.
LEHUA: One more thing, then the recap. The adaptive thing. The SAT is adaptive by module. Module one is a mix of easy, medium, and hard questions for everybody. Depending on how you do, module two is either the harder version or the easier version, and the harder version can score higher. So what does that mean for the clock?
DEREK: It means module one accuracy matters more than module one speed. Do not sprint module one to save time. There's no saving time, each module has its own clock. Get module one right, calmly, and you unlock the module that can give you the big score.
LEHUA: Kaden, recap. Your words.
KADEN: Two passes. First pass in order. If I can't see the path in about ten seconds, I guess, flag it, and go. Second pass, I upgrade the flags, closest one first, monster last. Check the clock twice, at one-third and two-thirds. Last minute, stop solving and fill the grid. Module one is about getting it right, not fast. And no blanks.
DEREK: That's the whole episode in one breath. Seven.
KADEN: Why not higher?
DEREK: You left out reading the question first.
LEHUA: Alright. Here's your homework. If you haven't done the placement check yet, do that first, it's two questions per skill and it tells the dashboard where to start you. Then go to Timed in the app. Do one Reading and Writing module, just one, with the checkpoints on. Don't worry about the score. Watch what the clock does to you. Then come back for episode four, Desmos.
KADEN: And flag stuff.
PONO: And flag stuff. No blanks.
DEREK: No blanks.
LEHUA: No blanks. That's episode three. Thanks for listening, everybody. Go catch your bus, Kaden.
KADEN: It left.
PONO: Should've flagged it.

choices: Yes, a quarter point per wrong answer
No, a blank is the only answer that is always wrong

choices: Keep working until you get it

Skip to the end of the module

sat.title: Desmos Is Your Co-pilot
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode four. I'm Lehua. Derek is here, Coach Pono is here, and Kaden is here and he's already holding his phone like a calculator.
KADEN: I'm ready for math. Mentally.
PONO: Mentally is the hard part. Good start.
LEHUA: Callback first. Kaden, last episode was the time squeeze. Give me the plan in three pieces.
KADEN: Two passes. First pass, if I can't see the path in about ten seconds, I guess, flag it, and move on. Check the clock twice, at the one-third mark and the two-thirds mark. And no blanks.
PONO: That's it. Clean.
LEHUA: Okay. Today is Desmos. Derek, set it up.
DEREK: On the digital SAT, there's a Desmos graphing calculator built into Bluebook. It's there for the whole Math section, both modules. You can still bring your own approved calculator, but most students should learn the built-in one, because it's always there and it graphs.
KADEN: So it's like the game gives you a free power-up and most people never press the button.
DEREK: That's exactly it. And the power-up is this. If you can turn a question into equations, Desmos can draw them, and the answer is often a point you can tap.
LEHUA: Give me the big one.
DEREK: Systems of equations. Two lines. The question asks where they cross, or for the values that make both equations true. Same thing. Type the first equation on one line in Desmos, type the second on the next line, and look for where the lines meet. Tap that point. Desmos shows you the coordinates.
PONO: Okay, let's try one. Listen up, this one is short. I'll read it twice.
PONO: "The line y equals two x plus one and the line y equals negative x plus seven cross at the point x comma y. What is the value of y?" A, two. B, three. C, five. D, seven.
PONO: One more time. "The line y equals two x plus one and the line y equals negative x plus seven cross at the point x comma y. What is the value of y?" A, two. B, three. C, five. D, seven.
LEHUA: Pause it and try. Algebra or Desmos, your choice.
LEHUA: Okay, we're back. Kaden?
KADEN: I set them equal. Two x plus one equals negative x plus seven. Add x to both sides, three x plus one equals seven. Subtract one, three x equals six. x equals two. So A.
DEREK: Your algebra is perfect. Your answer is wrong.
KADEN: Bro. How.
DEREK: Read the last sentence of the question again. What did it ask for?
KADEN: The value of y. Oh no.
DEREK: Right. x is two. Now plug it back in. y equals two times two, plus one. That's five. The answer is C. And notice what they did. Two is sitting right there as choice A, waiting for you.
LEHUA: So that's the trap. Say the name.
DEREK: The app calls it answers the wrong part. You did real work, and you got a real number, but it's the answer to a question they didn't ask. With systems, the test loves to ask for y, or for x plus y, because they know a lot of students solve for x and stop.
PONO: Two habits fix it. Before you start, say out loud in your head what the question wants. Y. Then after you get a number, read the last sentence again before you tap anything.
DEREK: And here's how Desmos helps with this trap. Type both lines. Tap where they cross. Desmos shows two comma five. Both numbers are on the screen at the same time. Now you just pick the one they asked for.
KADEN: Okay, so Desmos is faster?
DEREK: For that one, about the same. Here's the honest part. Desmos is not always faster. Typing takes time. If the algebra is one or two steps, like three x plus four equals nineteen, just do it. You'll be done before you finish typing.
LEHUA: So when is Desmos the move?
DEREK: Three cases. One, systems where the numbers are messy, like fractions or decimals. Two, quadratics. If they ask for the solutions of x squared minus five x plus six equals zero, you can graph y equals that expression and tap where it crosses the x-axis. Those points, two and three, are the solutions. Three, checking. You solved it by hand, you have a little time left, so you graph it to confirm.
KADEN: What if the lines don't show up?
DEREK: Then zoom out. Sometimes the crossing is off the screen. If the lines look parallel, they might actually be parallel, which means no solution. That's a real answer choice sometimes.
PONO: Okay, here's how I think about it. Desmos is a good horse. A good horse knows the trail. But you still hold the reins. If you don't know where you're going, the horse just walks you in circles around the arena.
KADEN: Coach, every episode.
PONO: Every episode. And it's always true.
LEHUA: Derek, any typing tips? Because I've watched kids fight the keyboard for a minute on one equation.
DEREK: Three. Use parentheses more than you think you need. You don't need a times sign. Type two, then x, and Desmos reads it as two times x. And if a question uses letters other than x and y, rename them to x and y when you type, so it graphs like you expect.
LEHUA: And practice in the real thing.
DEREK: Yes. Open Bluebook before test day and play with the calculator. The free official practice is linked in the app under the official practice button. The first time you use Desmos should not be during the test.
LEHUA: The map app in my car works the same way. It's helpful, but only if I already know I'm going to Costco and not the other side of the island.
PONO: You going today?
LEHUA: It's Sunday. They close at six, and it's an hour away. I'm leaving right after this.
PONO: Then we go fast.
LEHUA: Kaden, recap for us. Your words.
KADEN: Okay. Desmos is built into Bluebook for all of Math. For a system, type both equations and tap where they cross, and that's your x and y. For a quadratic, graph it and tap where it hits the x-axis, those are the solutions. If the algebra is one or two steps, just do the algebra, because typing is slower. And the trap is answers the wrong part. I solved for x, but they wanted y. So say what they want before I start, and read the last sentence again before I pick.
DEREK: That's good. You even admitted the mistake in your own recap. Eight.
KADEN: I'll take eight.

PONO: And keep using your checkpoints. Desmos doesn't stop the clock.
LEHUA: That's episode four. Next time, episode five, read the question first, for Words in Context and Central Ideas. Thanks for listening, everybody.
KADEN: Drive safe.
LEHUA: Always.

sat.title: Read the Question First
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode five. I'm Lehua. Sarah is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here, and he made the bus today.
KADEN: I made the bus. I ran for it, but I made it. Driver waited like two seconds. Respect.
LEHUA: Okay, callback. Last episode was Desmos. Kaden, what was the trap, and what was the fix?
KADEN: Answers the wrong part. I solved for x and they wanted y. The fix is, say what the question wants before I start, and read the last sentence again before I pick.
DEREK: Good. That habit is going to show up again today, on the reading side.
LEHUA: Today is Reading and Writing. Sarah, it's yours.
SARAH: Today is one move. Predict, then match. It works on two kinds of questions. Words in Context, where there's a blank and you pick the word. And Central Ideas, where they ask what the passage is mostly saying.
SARAH: The move has three steps. First, read the question so you know what you're hunting for. Second, read the passage and make your own answer before you look at the choices. A word for a blank, or one short sentence for the main idea. Third, find the choice that matches your prediction.
KADEN: Why not just read the choices? They're right there.
SARAH: Because the choices are built to sound good. If you read them first, they plant ideas in your head. Four choices, and three of them were written to fool you. If you already have your own answer, you're comparing them to something solid instead of comparing them to each other.
DEREK: Same in math. You want your own number before you look at theirs.
LEHUA: Okay, let's try. Sarah, read it. No choices yet.
SARAH: Right. I'm going to read just the sentence twice. Your job is to come up with your own word for the blank. Here it is.
SARAH: "Researchers expected the new seedlings to struggle in the cold, but the plants proved surprisingly blank, surviving three frosts with little damage."
SARAH: Again. "Researchers expected the new seedlings to struggle in the cold, but the plants proved surprisingly blank, surviving three frosts with little damage."
LEHUA: Pause it and try. Say your own word out loud before we give you any choices.
LEHUA: And we're back. Kaden, your word?
KADEN: Tough.
SARAH: Tough is a great prediction. Where did you get it?
KADEN: It says they were supposed to struggle, but. So they didn't struggle. And they survived frosts.
SARAH: Exactly. Two clues. The word "but" flips the expectation, and "surviving three frosts" tells you which way it flipped. Now here are the choices. A, fragile. B, resilient. C, indestructible. D, colorful.
SARAH: Once more. A, fragile. B, resilient. C, indestructible. D, colorful.
KADEN: Okay. Fragile is out, that's the opposite of tough. Colorful is random. So it's resilient or indestructible.
SARAH: And which one matches "tough" better?
KADEN: Honestly indestructible sounds tougher.
SARAH: And that's the trap. Listen to the last part of the sentence again. "With little damage." Little damage is still some damage. Indestructible means nothing can hurt it at all. That's more than the sentence says.
DEREK: That's the app's trap name. Too extreme.
SARAH: Too extreme. The choice goes past what the text supports. It's the right direction, but it goes too far. Resilient means able to recover or hold up under stress. That matches tough, and it matches little damage. Plug it back in. "The plants proved surprisingly resilient, surviving three frosts with little damage." Reads right. The answer is B.
KADEN: So the trap was basically my own prediction, but louder.
SARAH: That's a perfect way to say it. Too extreme choices are the loud version of the right answer. Listen for words like always, never, completely, impossible, proves. Then go back and check whether the passage was really that strong.
LEHUA: Now the Central Ideas version. Same move, different target.
SARAH: For Central Ideas, you read the whole short passage, then say the main point in one short sentence, before the choices. Then you match. Two extra things to watch. A choice can be too narrow, which means it's about one detail, not the whole passage. Or it can be too broad, which means it covers more than this passage actually says.
SARAH: And too extreme shows up here a lot. The passage says a study suggests something, and the choice says the study proves it. Suggests and proves are not the same strength.
DEREK: In math terms, the passage said "probably." The choice said "always." That's a different number.
LEHUA: What about time? Kaden's going to ask.
KADEN: I was going to ask.
SARAH: The prediction takes about five seconds once you practice. It saves time, because you stop reading every choice three times. When you have your own word, two choices fall away right away.
LEHUA: And if you can't predict anything?
SARAH: Then predict the direction. Positive or negative. Strong or weak. Even that crosses out a choice or two. Then use what we did in episode two. Cross out with a reason.
KADEN: Okay, real question. Sarah, do you predict when you read texts from people?
SARAH: I predict where the commas should be. That's different. My mom texted the family chat, "Pick up milk eggs and rice." No commas. I asked her what a milk egg is.
LEHUA: Did she answer?
SARAH: She sent the list again. Same list. Still no commas.
LEHUA: Recap time. Kaden, go.
KADEN: Read the question first so I know what I'm hunting. Then read the passage and make my own answer before I look. One word for a blank, one short sentence for a main idea. Then match. The trap is too extreme. It's the right direction but louder than the passage, like indestructible when the passage said little damage. Watch for always, never, proves. And for main ideas, not too narrow, not too broad.
DEREK: That was solid. The "my prediction but louder" line was good. Eight.
KADEN: I keep getting eight.
DEREK: You keep earning eight.
LEHUA: Homework. In the app, go to Drill and pick Words in Context. Do ten. On every one, cover the choices with your hand, or just look away from the screen, and say your word out loud before you look. When you miss one and it says "Trap: too extreme," go back and find the part of the passage that was softer than the choice.
SARAH: And open the Strategies tab for Words in Context. The steps are right there.
LEHUA: That's episode five. Next time, episode six, is the smallest step, inferences and evidence. Thanks for listening, everybody.
SARAH: Kaden, prediction for your rating next episode?
KADEN: Eight.
DEREK: Don't predict my ratings.

sat.title: The Smallest Step
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode six. I'm Lehua. Sarah is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here, and he says he only slept a little.
KADEN: I was in a ranked match. It went to overtime. We lost. I don't want to talk about it.
SARAH: We'll talk about it a little.
LEHUA: Callback first. Kaden, last episode. What's the move, and what's the trap?
KADEN: Predict, then match. Make my own answer before I look at the choices. The trap was too extreme. Right direction, but louder than the passage. Like indestructible when it said little damage.
SARAH: Perfect. Hold on to "louder than the passage," because today is the cousin of that trap.
LEHUA: Today is inferences and evidence. Sarah, go.
SARAH: Inference questions on the SAT usually end with a blank and ask, "Which choice most logically completes the text?" The passage builds an argument, and you supply the last step. Here's the rule the whole episode hangs on. The right answer is the smallest step. Not the most interesting step. The smallest one.
KADEN: Why would they want the boring one?
SARAH: Because the boring one is the one the passage actually supports. The test is checking whether you can stay inside the text. Every interesting answer brings in something the passage never said.
SARAH: So here are the steps. Find the last line before the blank and ask what it sets up. Predict what has to come next. Then pick the choice that needs the fewest new ideas. Anything the text never gave you, cut.
LEHUA: Okay, let's try one. Sarah, read it twice.
SARAH: Here it is. "A town added new streetlights to Main Street but not to Oak Street. The next year, nighttime accidents dropped on Main Street and stayed about the same on Oak Street. This suggests that blank."
SARAH: Again. "A town added new streetlights to Main Street but not to Oak Street. The next year, nighttime accidents dropped on Main Street and stayed about the same on Oak Street. This suggests that blank."
SARAH: Predict first. Then here are the choices. A, the new streetlights may have helped reduce nighttime accidents on Main Street. B, drivers on Oak Street are more careless than drivers on Main Street. C, streetlights will end nighttime accidents in every town. D, the town will add streetlights to Oak Street next.
SARAH: One more time. A, the streetlights may have helped on Main Street. B, Oak Street drivers are more careless. C, streetlights will end accidents in every town. D, the town will add lights to Oak Street next.
LEHUA: Pause it and try. Find the smallest step.
LEHUA: And we're back. Kaden?
KADEN: My prediction was, the lights helped. But D sounds smart. If the lights worked, obviously they'd put them on Oak Street next.
SARAH: Great, because that's exactly the trap. Does the passage say anything about the town's plans?
KADEN: No. It just says what happened.
SARAH: Right. To pick D, you have to bring in a new idea, that the town is planning more lights. The app has a name for that. Adds an assumption. The choice needs one extra idea the passage never gave you.
DEREK: B does the same thing. Nothing in the passage is about how careful the drivers are. You'd have to invent that.
SARAH: And C should sound familiar.
KADEN: Every town. That's too extreme. Last episode's trap.
SARAH: Exactly. One street in one town does not prove anything about every town. So we're left with A. And look at the word "may." The streetlights may have helped. That's soft, and soft is what the evidence earns. One street got lights, accidents dropped there, and the other street stayed the same. The smallest step is, the lights might be part of why. The answer is A.
KADEN: So my prediction was right, and then I talked myself out of it.
SARAH: That happens a lot. The trap choice is usually the one that feels clever. When a choice makes you think, "Oh, and then they would," ask yourself where the passage said that.
LEHUA: Okay, the evidence questions. Those are different, right?
SARAH: They're flipped. Inference gives you the evidence and asks for the claim. Command of Evidence gives you the claim and asks for the evidence. The steps are, find the exact claim the question wants supported. Say it in your own words. Then test each choice. Does this prove this claim directly? A true statement that doesn't support the claim is still wrong.
LEHUA: And some of those have a chart.
DEREK: That's mine. Some evidence questions give you a table or a graph, and the choices quote numbers from it. Three checks. Read the labels, read the units, then check the exact numbers against the claim.
DEREK: Quick one, no pause. Say the claim is, "Nighttime accidents on Main Street fell by more than half." A choice says accidents went from forty to twenty-two. Does that support the claim?
KADEN: It went down a lot, so yes?
DEREK: Half of forty is twenty. Twenty-two is more than twenty. So it fell by less than half. The number is real, the chart is real, and the choice still doesn't support this claim. You have to do the arithmetic.
LEHUA: So the number is true. It just doesn't prove the point.
DEREK: Right. True, and still the wrong answer.
SARAH: And on the chart questions, the passage still matters. The claim comes from the text. The chart is just the proof. Read the claim first, then go to the chart looking for one thing.
LEHUA: Sarah, real question. Did you read anything this week with a bad inference in it?
SARAH: My mom texted, "Your brother didn't call, so he must be mad at me." That is a huge assumption. Also she put a comma before "so," which is correct, and I was so proud I forgot to answer the actual question.
LEHUA: Was he mad?
SARAH: His phone was dead.
LEHUA: Recap time. Kaden.
KADEN: On "most logically completes," the right answer is the smallest step, not the most exciting one. Find the last line, predict, pick the choice that needs the fewest new ideas. The trap is adds an assumption, like saying the town will put lights on Oak Street next when the passage never said that. Watch for soft words like may, because soft is what the evidence earns. For evidence questions, it's the other way. Say the claim in my own words, then find the choice that proves that exact claim. On charts, check the labels, the units, and do the math.
DEREK: You got the chart part, and you admitted you talked yourself out of the right answer. Eight.
KADEN: I'll take eight.
LEHUA: Homework. In the app, go to Drill and pick Inferences. Do ten. On each one, say your prediction before you look, and when you miss one and it says "Trap: adds an assumption," find the extra idea the choice snuck in. Then open the Strategies tab for Inferences and read the four steps.
SARAH: And say the extra idea out loud. It sounds ridiculous once you say it.
LEHUA: That's episode six. Next time, episode seven, where the sentence breaks. Punctuation. Sarah's favorite.
SARAH: It's my birthday and my wedding in one episode.
LEHUA: I gotta run. The record store in town just got a new box of old vinyl, and my cousin is already parked outside. Thanks for listening, everybody.

The choice that mentions the most details

A claim says accidents fell by more than half. A chart choice shows 40 falling to 22. Does it support the claim?

Yes, because the number comes from the chart

sat.title: Where the Sentence Breaks
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode seven. I'm Lehua. Derek is here, Kaden is here, and Sarah is here, and she's been waiting all season for this one.
SARAH: All season. I brought a list.
KADEN: She brought a printed list.
LEHUA: Callback first. Kaden, last episode. What's the right answer on a "most logically completes" question?
KADEN: The smallest step. Not the exciting one. And the trap was adds an assumption, when the choice needs an idea the passage never gave me. Like the town putting lights on Oak Street.
SARAH: Good. Today we go from ideas to punctuation. Same kind of discipline, though. You look at what's actually on the page.
LEHUA: Today is Boundaries. Sarah, the floor is yours.
SARAH: Boundaries questions ask what punctuation goes between two parts of a sentence. And here's the good news. You don't need to know every rule in the grammar book. You need one move. Label both sides.
SARAH: Find where the punctuation goes. Then look at the words on the left and ask, could this stand alone as a complete sentence? Then do the same on the right. Each side is either independent, which means it's a complete sentence, or it isn't. A dependent clause or a fragment can't stand alone.
KADEN: How do I know if it's complete?
SARAH: It needs a subject and a verb, and it has to make sense by itself. "She still had to print it" is complete. "Because she still had to print it" is not. That word "because" makes it lean on something else.
DEREK: It's like checking both sides of an equation before you touch anything.
SARAH: Exactly. Once both sides are labeled, the punctuation picks itself. If both sides are independent, you have three standard choices. A period. A semicolon. Or a comma plus a joining word like and, but, or so. What you can't use is a comma alone.
LEHUA: And that's called?
SARAH: A comma splice. Two complete sentences glued together with just a comma. It's the most common wrong answer in this whole skill.
LEHUA: Okay, let's try one. Sarah, read it twice.
SARAH: Here's the sentence. When I say blank, that's where the punctuation goes. "Maya finished her essay at midnight blank she still had to print it."
SARAH: Again. "Maya finished her essay at midnight blank she still had to print it."
SARAH: The choices. A, a comma after midnight. B, a semicolon after midnight. C, no punctuation at all. D, no punctuation after midnight, and a comma after she.
SARAH: One more time. A, comma. B, semicolon. C, nothing. D, nothing after midnight, comma after she.
LEHUA: Pause it and try. Label both sides first.
LEHUA: And we're back. Kaden?
KADEN: I said A, the comma. Because when I read it out loud, there's a little pause right there. Midnight, pause, she still had to print it.
SARAH: That pause is real. And that's exactly why this trap works. Let's label. Left side. "Maya finished her essay at midnight." Complete sentence?
KADEN: Yeah. Subject is Maya, verb is finished.
SARAH: Right side. "She still had to print it."
KADEN: Also complete. Oh. So it's two sentences.
SARAH: Two independent clauses. So a comma alone can't hold them. That's a comma splice. In the app, that trap is called near miss. It looks almost right, and it has one small error. It sounds right when you say it, because your voice pauses at commas and periods the same way.
DEREK: So "it sounds fine" is not a test.
SARAH: Not on Boundaries. Your ear is great for a lot of grammar. It's bad at telling a comma from a period. Now, C, no punctuation, runs the two sentences together with nothing. That's wrong too. D puts a comma between the subject, she, and the verb, had. You never split a subject from its verb with one comma. So the answer is B, the semicolon. Two complete sides, and a semicolon is one of the three standard ways to join them.
KADEN: What if there were a choice with a comma and "but"?
SARAH: Then that would also be correct, which is why you won't see both in the same question. Each question has only one correct option.
LEHUA: Okay, colons and dashes. People are scared of those.
SARAH: Two quick rules. A colon comes after a complete sentence, and it introduces something. An explanation, an example, or a list. "She had one job left: printing the essay." The left side has to be complete. The right side doesn't have to be, but it can be, as long as it explains the left side.
SARAH: Dashes come in pairs when they set off extra information, like a pair of commas. "Maya, my cousin, finished at midnight." You could write that with two dashes instead of two commas. What you can't do is open with a dash and close with a comma. Pick one and match it.
DEREK: Matching pairs. That one I like.
SARAH: And one more. If the sentence opens with a dependent clause, like "Because she finished late," you put a comma after it, then the main clause. "Because she finished late, she printed it in the morning."
LEHUA: So the semicolon rule is?
SARAH: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides. Every time. If one side is dependent, a semicolon is wrong.
KADEN: This is like my car. My mom says I can't merge until I check both mirrors. Left side, right side, then go.
SARAH: That is the best thing you've ever said on this show.
LEHUA: Sarah, I know you have a story. You always have a story.
SARAH: My mom texted the family chat, "Dinner is at six, I made your favorite." Comma splice. Two complete sentences, one comma. I replied with a semicolon.
LEHUA: Just the semicolon?
SARAH: Just the semicolon. She replied, "Is that a winking face?"
LEHUA: Recap. Kaden, go.
KADEN: Find where the punctuation goes and label both sides. Complete sentence or not. If both sides are complete, I need a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a word like and, but, or so. A comma alone is a comma splice, and that's the near miss trap. It sounds fine out loud because I pause there, so I can't trust my ear. A semicolon needs complete sentences on both sides. A colon needs a complete sentence before it. When dashes or commas set off extra information, they come in matching pairs.
DEREK: Clean. And the mirrors line was good. Nine.
KADEN: Nine. I'm going to frame that.
LEHUA: Homework. In the app, go to Drill and pick Boundaries. Do ten. On every one, before you look at the choices, say "left side complete" or "left side not," then the same for the right. When you miss one and it says "Trap: near miss," check whether you trusted the pause.
SARAH: And read the Strategies tab for Boundaries. It's four steps. Four.
LEHUA: That's episode seven. Next time, episode eight, however, therefore, for example. Transitions. I'm out. I have paddling practice at the harbor, and if I'm late, I'm the one bailing water.
KADEN: Paddle fast.
LEHUA: Always. Thanks for listening, everybody.

Label each side as a complete sentence or not

sat.title: However, Therefore, For Example
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode eight. I'm Lehua. Sarah is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here, and he's eating a granola bar like it owes him money.
KADEN: I didn't have breakfast. This is breakfast.
LEHUA: Callback first. Kaden, last episode. Two complete sentences, and a comma between them. What's that called, and what's the trap?
KADEN: A comma splice. The trap is near miss, because it sounds right when I say it out loud. So I label both sides first. Complete or not.
SARAH: Love it. And today is still about how sentences connect. Last time it was the punctuation between them. Today it's the words.
LEHUA: Transitions. Sarah, go.
SARAH: Transition questions give you two sentences with a blank at the start of the second one, and four choices, words like however, therefore, for example, in addition. Here's the move. Before you look at the choices, name the relationship between the sentences. There are really only five. Add, which means more of the same. Contrast, which means it goes against what came before. Cause, which means the second one is a result of the first. Example, which means the second one gives an example of the first. And sequence, which means it comes next in time.
KADEN: Why can't I just try each word and see which one sounds smooth?
SARAH: Because they all sound smooth. That's the whole trick. Transition words are built to flow. "Therefore" sounds great in almost any sentence. The question isn't which word sounds good. It's which word means the right relationship.
DEREK: It's like a plus or minus sign. The numbers don't change, but the sign changes the whole answer.
LEHUA: Okay, let's try one. Sarah, read it twice.
SARAH: Here it is. "The team practiced every morning for a month. Blank, they lost their first game by twenty points."
SARAH: Again. "The team practiced every morning for a month. Blank, they lost their first game by twenty points."
SARAH: Before the choices, name the relationship. Then here they are. A, therefore. B, nevertheless. C, for example. D, in addition.
SARAH: One more time. A, therefore. B, nevertheless. C, for example. D, in addition.
LEHUA: Pause it and try. Name the relationship first.
LEHUA: And we're back. Kaden, what's the relationship?
KADEN: Honestly, I almost said therefore. They practiced, therefore, something happened.
SARAH: That's the one the test hopes you pick. What would you expect after a month of practice every morning?
KADEN: That they'd play well. That they'd win, or at least not get destroyed.
SARAH: And what actually happened?
KADEN: They lost by twenty. Oh. So it went against what you'd expect. That's contrast.
SARAH: Contrast. Now cut every choice that isn't contrast. "Therefore" is cause. It says the loss happened because of the practice, which flips the meaning. In the app, that trap is called opposite. It's the right topic, pointing the wrong direction. "For example" is example, and the loss isn't an example of practicing. "In addition" is add. So the only contrast word left is B, nevertheless. Nevertheless means "even so," or "in spite of that." In spite of all the practice, they lost. The answer is B.
KADEN: So "therefore" was basically the opposite of the right answer.
SARAH: Exactly. Cause and contrast pull in opposite directions. One says, "and so, as expected." The other says, "but, against what you'd expect." When you see two choices from opposite categories, one of them is usually the trap.
LEHUA: What if two choices are in the same category? Like however and nevertheless?
SARAH: Usually the test won't put two words with the same meaning in one question. If it does, one of them fits the exact shade better. That's step four. Pick the word that fits the exact meaning. But most of the time, once you cut the wrong categories, you're down to one.
KADEN: It's like a combo in a fighting game. The next move depends on what you just did. You can't just mash buttons.
SARAH: That's a good one. Don't button-mash transitions.
LEHUA: Now the notes questions. Those look scary.
SARAH: They look long, and they're actually fast. You get a list of bullet-point notes a student took, and the question says, "The student wants to do something. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?" The move is, read the goal first. Before any of the notes.
DEREK: Read the question first. That one keeps coming back.
SARAH: Because it keeps working. Say the goal is, "emphasize a similarity between two programs." Every choice will use real facts from the notes. Every single one is accurate. The right one is the one that does the goal. If a choice explains how one program started, it's true, it's from the notes, and it doesn't show a similarity. Cut it.
KADEN: So you don't even have to read all the notes.
SARAH: You can skim them. The answer is decided by the goal. Circle the key words of the goal, like "similarity" or "contrast" or "introduce the study to a new audience," and find the choice that does exactly that.
LEHUA: Sarah, any punctuation drama in your life this week?
SARAH: My cousin's wedding program said, "Thank you to my parents, the band and the caterer." No comma after band. So, according to the program, her parents are the band and the caterer.
LEHUA: Wait, is that comma even required?
SARAH: No. It's a style choice, and the SAT doesn't make you pick a side on it. But it's my style choice.
LEHUA: Did you tell her?
SARAH: At the reception. She said, "Sarah, eat your cake." Lovely wedding.
LEHUA: Recap. Kaden.
KADEN: On transitions, name the relationship before I look. Add, contrast, cause, example, or sequence. Then cut every choice from the wrong category. The trap is opposite, like picking therefore when the sentences contrast, because the team practiced and still lost. Don't pick the one that sounds smooth, because they all sound smooth. On the notes questions, read the goal first, circle it, and pick the choice that does that goal. True facts that do a different job are still wrong.
DEREK: Organized, and you got both question types. Eight.
KADEN: Solid.
LEHUA: Homework. In the app, go to Drill and pick Transitions. Do ten. On every one, say the relationship out loud before you look at the choices. When you miss one and it says "Trap: opposite," figure out which direction you flipped.
SARAH: Then try a few Rhetorical Synthesis items. Read the goal, nothing else, and see if you can guess the kind of answer before you read the notes.

sat.title: Lines Are Rates
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode nine. I'm Lehua. Derek is here, Coach Pono is here, and Kaden is here, and he drove himself today.
KADEN: I drove myself. My gas light came on in the parking lot. Every mile, the tank goes down the same amount, and so does my bank account.
DEREK: That's a linear function. You just taught the first half of the episode.
LEHUA: Hold that. Callback first. Kaden, last episode was transitions. What do you do before you look at the choices?
KADEN: Name the relationship. Add, contrast, cause, example, or sequence. Then cut every choice from the wrong category. The trap was opposite, like picking therefore when the team practiced and still lost.
PONO: Good. Today we're back to math, but the habit is the same. Say what's going on before you start moving.
LEHUA: Lines are rates. Derek.
DEREK: Here's the whole idea in one sentence. Almost every linear word problem on the SAT is a starting amount plus a rate. Something starts somewhere, and it changes by the same amount every step. That's a line.
DEREK: In y equals m x plus b, b is where you start. That's the y-intercept. And m is the rate, how much y changes every time x goes up by one. That's the slope. Here's the habit. Say the slope in words, with units. Not "slope is negative three." Say "negative three gallons per minute." If you can say it in words, you understand the problem.
KADEN: Why does saying it out loud matter?
DEREK: Because the most common mistake on these is swapping the slope and the starting value. If you say the units, you can hear which number is which. Forty gallons is an amount. Three gallons per minute is a rate.
PONO: Okay, let's try one. I'll read it twice. Short one.
PONO: "A water tank holds forty gallons. It drains at three gallons per minute. How many gallons are left after eight minutes?" A, sixteen. B, twenty-six. C, thirty-seven. D, sixty-four.
PONO: One more time. "A water tank holds forty gallons. It drains at three gallons per minute. How many gallons are left after eight minutes?" A, sixteen. B, twenty-six. C, thirty-seven. D, sixty-four.
LEHUA: Pause it and try. Find the start and the rate first.
LEHUA: And we're back. Kaden?
KADEN: Start is forty. Rate is negative three gallons per minute. So it's forty minus three times eight. Three times eight is twenty-four. Forty minus twenty-four is twenty-six. B.
DEREK: Your setup is perfect. Do the last subtraction again, slowly.
KADEN: Forty minus twenty-four. Zero minus four, I can't, so I borrow. Ten minus four is six. Then three minus two is one. Sixteen. Oh, come on.
DEREK: The answer is A, sixteen. And that's the trap. The app calls it calculation slip. You knew exactly what to do, and one small arithmetic step went wrong. Twenty-six is sitting there as choice B because borrowing and then forgetting to lower the tens digit is a common slip.
PONO: And look at the other two. Thirty-seven is forty minus three. That's one minute, not eight. Sixty-four is forty plus twenty-four. That's adding when the tank drains.
DEREK: Here's the fix for calculation slip. Check by going backward. If sixteen is left and twenty-four drained out, sixteen plus twenty-four should be forty. It is. Twenty-six plus twenty-four is fifty, which is more water than the tank started with. That check takes three seconds.
KADEN: So the check is just doing it in reverse.
DEREK: Right. Subtraction, check with addition. Division, check with multiplication. Or type it into Desmos if it's messy.
LEHUA: Now, backsolving. What's that?
DEREK: When the choices are numbers and the question asks for a value, you can test the choices instead of solving. Start with a middle choice, because if it's too big or too small, you know which way to move.
DEREK: Same tank. Say the question is, "After how many minutes will ten gallons be left?" And the choices are six, eight, ten, and twelve. Start with eight. Forty minus three times eight is sixteen. Sixteen gallons is too much water left, so you need more time. Move up. Try ten. Forty minus thirty is ten. Done. Ten minutes.
PONO: That's how you work a young horse. You don't guess the whole trail. You try one step, you see if he goes left or right, and you adjust.
KADEN: Coach, there's always a horse.
PONO: There's always a horse.
LEHUA: And plugging in?
DEREK: That one is for when the answer choices have letters in them. Pick a simple number, like two or three, for the letter. Work the problem with your number to get a target. Then put the same number into each choice and see which one hits the target.
DEREK: Same tank. Say the question asks which expression gives the gallons left after t minutes. Pick t equals two. Two minutes drains six gallons, so thirty-four are left. That's the target. Now test the choices. Forty minus three t, with t equals two, is thirty-four. Hit. Forty plus three t is forty-six. Miss. It turns algebra into arithmetic.
LEHUA: And systems?
DEREK: Two lines, two rates. Like two tanks draining at different speeds, and the question is when they hold the same amount. That's where the lines cross. Episode four has the whole Desmos method. Type both, tap where they cross, and read the part they asked for.
KADEN: Okay, how do I know which number is the slope when it's a graph?
DEREK: Pick two points. Rise over run. How far up or down, divided by how far across. And keep the order the same on top and bottom. If you flip it, you get run over rise, which is the other common mistake.
PONO: Remember the clock, too. Math averages about ninety-five seconds a question. Setup in your head, write the numbers, check backward. If the setup isn't there in ten seconds, guess, flag, move.
LEHUA: Recap. Kaden, go.
KADEN: A linear word problem is a starting amount plus a rate. Say the slope in words with units, like negative three gallons per minute, so I don't swap the start and the rate. The trap was calculation slip. I set it up right and then messed up the subtraction. The fix is to check backward, sixteen plus twenty-four is forty. If the choices are numbers, backsolve, start in the middle, and move the right way. If the choices have letters, plug in my own numbers. And for slope off a graph, rise over run, same order.
DEREK: You owned the slip and you fixed it out loud. Eight.
KADEN: I'll take it. I even checked it backward.
LEHUA: Homework. In the app, go to Drill and pick linear functions and graphs. Do ten. On each one, say the slope in words with units before you pick. When you miss one and it says "Trap: calculation slip," redo the arithmetic backward and find the exact step.
PONO: And check one answer on every page by going backward. Make it a habit, not a rescue.
LEHUA: That's episode nine. Next time, episode ten, percent, ratio, and the mean versus the median. I gotta go, it's Wednesday, and the food trucks at the stables run out of the good stuff early.
PONO: Pukalani. Bring me back one plate.
LEHUA: You'll have to fight me for it. Thanks for listening, everybody.

sat.title: Percent, Ratio, and the Mean vs the Median
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode ten. Double digits. I'm Lehua. Derek is here, Sarah is here, and Kaden is here, and he says he has a confession.
KADEN: I bought a skin in a game last night because it said thirty percent off. Then I found out they raised the price first.
DEREK: You just walked into today's episode on purpose.
LEHUA: Callback first. Kaden, last episode. What's the habit with slope, and what's the fix for a calculation slip?
KADEN: Say the slope in words with units, like negative three gallons per minute. And for a calculation slip, check it backward. Sixteen plus twenty-four should be forty.
DEREK: Good. Today, backward checks still help. But the bigger risk is reading the question wrong.
LEHUA: Percent, ratio, mean and median. Derek.
DEREK: Three ideas today. First, percents are multipliers. Second, repeated percents grow differently than adding. Third, the mean and the median are not the same thing. Let's start with the first one.
DEREK: A twenty percent increase means multiply by one point two. A twenty percent decrease means multiply by point eight. Don't add and subtract percents. Turn every percent change into a multiplier, and if there are two changes in a row, multiply in order. And when the question asks for percent change, it's the difference divided by the original. Always the original.
SARAH: Can I add something from the reading side? Every word of a percent question matters. Of what? Of the original, or of the new price? A lot of the misses on these are reading misses, not math misses.
LEHUA: Okay, let's try one. Derek, read it twice.
DEREK: "A jacket costs one hundred dollars. The price goes up twenty percent. Then the new price goes down twenty percent. What is the final price?" A, one hundred dollars. B, ninety-six dollars. C, eighty dollars. D, one hundred four dollars.
DEREK: One more time. "A jacket costs one hundred dollars. The price goes up twenty percent. Then the new price goes down twenty percent. What is the final price?" A, one hundred. B, ninety-six. C, eighty. D, one hundred four.
LEHUA: Pause it and try.
LEHUA: And we're back. Kaden?
KADEN: Up twenty is a hundred twenty. Down twenty is back to a hundred. A. It went up and came back down.
DEREK: How much did you take off the hundred twenty?
KADEN: Twenty dollars. Twenty percent of a hundred.
SARAH: Read the question one more time. "Then the new price goes down twenty percent."
KADEN: The new price. Oh. So it's twenty percent of a hundred twenty, not of a hundred.
DEREK: Right. Use multipliers. One hundred times one point two is one hundred twenty. One hundred twenty times point eight is ninety-six. The answer is B, ninety-six dollars. Up twenty and down twenty is not even. You end up four percent lower.
DEREK: And the trap has a name. The app calls it misread the question. Your math was fine. You took twenty percent of the wrong number because you read past "the new price."
SARAH: That's why I care. The words "the new price" were the whole question.
LEHUA: What about ratios? Same thing?
DEREK: Same idea, multiply and track units. If a recipe uses two cups of rice for every three cups of water, write the units next to the numbers. Two cups rice over three cups water. If you need cups of water for four cups of rice, set it up so cups of rice cancel. Four cups rice times three cups water over two cups rice is six cups water. If the units don't cancel to what the question asks for, the setup is wrong.
LEHUA: Okay, the second idea. Growth.
DEREK: Linear growth adds the same amount every step. Exponential growth multiplies by the same number every step. If a town has a hundred people and grows by ten people a year, that's linear. A hundred ten, a hundred twenty, a hundred thirty. If it grows by ten percent a year, that's exponential. Multiply by one point one each year. A hundred ten, then a hundred twenty-one.
KADEN: Those look almost the same.
DEREK: For two years, yes. Wait twenty years and they're not even close. Linear gets to three hundred. Ten percent a year gets to about six hundred seventy. A lot of the time, the SAT question is just, which kind is it? Same amount each step means linear. Same percent each step means exponential.
LEHUA: And the third one. Mean versus median.
DEREK: The mean is the average. Add everything, divide by how many. The median is the middle number when you line them up in order. They're often close. But one weird number, an outlier, pulls the mean and barely touches the median.
DEREK: Kaden's quiz scores. Eight, nine, nine, ten, and a zero, because he missed that one.
KADEN: I was sick. I'm not sick now. Keep going.
DEREK: Add them. Eight plus nine plus nine plus ten plus zero is thirty-six. Divide by five. The mean is seven point two. Line them up. Zero, eight, nine, nine, ten. The middle is nine. The median is nine.
SARAH: So which one describes Kaden better?
DEREK: The median. Most of his scores are around nine. The zero dragged the mean down. When the question says a data set has an outlier and asks what happens, the mean moves more than the median.
LEHUA: And remember episode one. The one thousand twenty-nine national number for the class of twenty twenty-five is a mean.
DEREK: Which is why we said average, not middle.
LEHUA: Sarah, I know there's a punctuation thing coming.
SARAH: My mom texted, "I'm at the store, prices are up twenty percent." Comma splice. But I let it go, because she was right about the prices.
LEHUA: Growth.
SARAH: Personal growth.
LEHUA: Recap. Kaden.
KADEN: Percents are multipliers. Up twenty is times one point two, down twenty is times point eight, and two changes in a row means multiply in order. Up twenty then down twenty gives ninety-six, not a hundred. The trap is misread the question. I took twenty percent of the old price when it said the new price. For ratios, write the units and make them cancel. Same amount each step is linear, same percent each step is exponential. Mean is the average, median is the middle, and an outlier pulls the mean a lot more than the median.
DEREK: All three ideas, in order, and the trap. Nine.
KADEN: Nine. Let's go.
LEHUA: Homework. In the app, go to Drill and pick percentages and percent change. Do ten. On every one, before you calculate, say out loud what the percent is of. The original or the new amount. When you miss one and it says "Trap: misread the question," find the exact words you read past.
SARAH: And underline them. In your head is fine.
LEHUA: That's episode ten. Next time, episode eleven, quadratics and the reference sheet. I need to sleep early. I'm doing the Saturday morning hike up to the pond, and my friends want to leave before it's light out.
KADEN: How early?
LEHUA: Early enough that I'm already tired. Thanks for listening, everybody.

sat.title: Quadratics and the Reference Sheet
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode eleven. I'm Lehua. Derek is here, Coach Pono is here, and Kaden is here, and he says he's been dreading this one.
KADEN: Quadratics. The word alone. It sounds like a dinosaur.
DEREK: It's one shape. A U, or an upside-down U. That's it.
LEHUA: Callback first. Kaden, last episode. A price goes up twenty percent, then the new price goes down twenty percent. Where do you end up?
KADEN: Ninety-six, if it started at a hundred. Times one point two, then times point eight. The trap was misread the question, because I took twenty percent of the old price.
PONO: Good. You remembered the words that mattered. Today has words that matter too.
LEHUA: Quadratics and the reference sheet. Derek.
DEREK: Three things today. The forms of a quadratic, what's on the reference sheet, and how to type answers when there are no choices. First, the forms. A quadratic can be written three ways, and each one hands you a different answer for free. Your job is to ask what they want, then pick the form that shows it.
DEREK: Vertex form looks like a, times the quantity x minus h, squared, plus k. The vertex is the point h comma k. If the number in front is negative, the U is upside down, so k is the maximum. If it's positive, k is the minimum.
DEREK: Factored form looks like x minus p, times x minus q. Those p and q are the roots, the x-values where y equals zero. Watch the sign. x minus four means the root is positive four. x plus one means the root is negative one.
DEREK: And standard form, a x squared plus b x plus c. The c by itself is the y-intercept.
PONO: Okay, let's try one. Listen up, I'll read it twice.
PONO: "A ball's height in feet, t seconds after it is thrown, is h equals negative two times the quantity t minus three, squared, plus fifty. What is the maximum height of the ball, in feet?" A, two. B, three. C, forty-seven. D, fifty.
PONO: One more time. "A ball's height in feet is h equals negative two times the quantity t minus three, squared, plus fifty. What is the maximum height of the ball, in feet?" A, two. B, three. C, forty-seven. D, fifty.
LEHUA: Pause it and try.
LEHUA: And we're back. Kaden?
KADEN: It's vertex form. Negative in front, so it's upside down, so there's a max. The vertex is three comma fifty. So, three. B.
DEREK: Everything you just said is right, up until the last word. What did the question ask for?
KADEN: The maximum height. In feet. Not the time. Bro. It's fifty. D.
DEREK: D, fifty feet. Three is when the ball hits its max. Three seconds. Fifty is how high it gets. The app calls this trap answers the wrong part. You found a real number from the problem, but it answers "when," and they asked "how high."
PONO: We saw this one in episode four, with x and y. Same trap, new costume.
KADEN: So the vertex gives me two answers and I have to pick the one they asked for.
DEREK: Right. The x part of the vertex is when, or where. The y part is the max or min. Say the units. "Three seconds" and "fifty feet" sound different. That's how you catch it.
KADEN: It's like the top of a jump in a game. There's when you hit the top, and how high you got. Different numbers.
DEREK: Exactly that.
LEHUA: Okay, the reference sheet. What's on it?
DEREK: In Bluebook, there's a reference sheet you can open any time in the Math section. It has the area and volume formulas, like circles, rectangles, triangles, cylinders, spheres, cones. It has the Pythagorean theorem. It has the two special right triangles, thirty-sixty-ninety and forty-five-forty-five-ninety. And it tells you the angles in a triangle add to one hundred eighty degrees, and a circle has three hundred sixty degrees, which is two pi radians.
LEHUA: So you don't have to memorize any of that.
DEREK: You should still know them, because opening the sheet costs time. But you don't have to panic. Here's what's not on the sheet. The trig ratios. SOH CAH TOA. Sine is opposite over hypotenuse. Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse. Tangent is opposite over adjacent. Memorize that one.
PONO: Okay, last thing. The ones with no choices.
DEREK: About a quarter of the Math questions are student-produced response. You type the answer in a box. Same rule as always, no guessing penalty, so never leave it empty. A few typing rules. You get up to five characters for a positive answer, six for a negative one, because the minus sign counts. If a fraction is too long, type it as a decimal. Don't type a mixed number like two and a half as two space one slash two. Type five slash two, or two point five. Don't type a dollar sign, a percent sign, or a comma. And if more than one answer works, type just one.
KADEN: What if I get a weird decimal?
DEREK: If it's too long for the box, round it or cut it off at the fourth digit so it fits. And check it in Desmos. If you graph the quadratic and tap the vertex or the crossing points, you can see the numbers. That's a good way to catch an answer that's the wrong part, too. The point shows both coordinates, and you pick the one they asked for.
PONO: Here's how I think about the vertex. When you rope a calf, there's a moment at the top of the throw where the rope just hangs. That's your vertex. When it hangs, and how high it hangs. Two different things. Don't tell me when if I asked you how high.
KADEN: Coach, that's the most specific one yet.
PONO: Gotta keep you guys awake.
LEHUA: Recap. Kaden, go.
KADEN: Pick the form that shows what they want. Vertex form for the max or min, factored form for the roots, standard form's last number for the y-intercept. Watch signs, x minus four means positive four. The trap is answers the wrong part. The vertex was three comma fifty, three was the time, and they wanted the height, so fifty. Say the units. The reference sheet has area and volume, Pythagorean theorem, special right triangles, one-eighty in a triangle, three-sixty in a circle. It does not have SOH CAH TOA. For typed answers, five characters, six if negative, no mixed numbers, no symbols, and never leave it blank.
DEREK: You caught your own mistake, and you got the grid-in rules. Eight.
KADEN: I'll take eight.
LEHUA: Homework. In the app, go to Drill and pick quadratics. Do ten. Before you solve each one, say which form you need. When you miss one and it says "Trap: answers the wrong part," write down what they asked for, with units, next to what you answered.
PONO: And open the reference sheet once before test day, so you know where everything is.
LEHUA: That's episode eleven. Next time, episode twelve, the error log habit. I'm out. My friend saved me a slice of the chocolate cake at the barbecue place on the main road, and she said she'd wait ten minutes. She has never waited ten minutes.
PONO: Fish and the Hog. Go. Run.
LEHUA: Thanks for listening, everybody.
