sat.title: The Error Log Habit
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode twelve. I'm Lehua. Coach Pono is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here, and he brought a notebook. An actual paper notebook.
KADEN: My mom bought it. She said if I'm going to be on a podcast, I should look like a student.
PONO: Looks good on you.
LEHUA: Callback first. Kaden, last episode. A quadratic in vertex form, with a negative in front. Where's the max, and what was the trap?
KADEN: The max is the k, the y part of the vertex. The trap was answers the wrong part. I said three, which was the time, when they asked for the height, which was fifty.
DEREK: Good. And notice you remember that mistake better than anything else from that episode.
KADEN: Because it was embarrassing.
DEREK: Exactly. That's today's whole episode.
LEHUA: The error log habit. Coach.
PONO: Okay, listen up, this one is important. Most students practice like this. Do twenty questions, look at the score, feel good or feel bad, close the app. That's like shooting free throws and only counting the makes. The questions you got right didn't teach you much. The ones you missed are where the points are.
PONO: So here's the habit. Every miss gets sorted into one of three buckets. Careless. Concept. Or time. And each bucket has a different fix.
DEREK: Careless means you knew how to do it and slipped. A sign, a subtraction, a misread word. Concept means you didn't know the rule or the method. Time means you rushed or guessed because the clock was running.
LEHUA: And the app asks you, right?
PONO: Right. When you miss a drill question, the app asks, "Why did you miss it?" and gives you three buttons. Careless. Didn't know it. Rushed. Be honest. Nobody sees it but you.
KADEN: What if I don't know which one?
PONO: That's what the example is for. Derek, give him one.
DEREK: Here's a real-sounding miss. I'll read it twice. "The question was, what is fifteen percent of eighty? The student wrote point one five times eighty and got fourteen. The correct answer is twelve." Which bucket?
DEREK: Again. "What is fifteen percent of eighty? The student wrote point one five times eighty and got fourteen. The correct answer is twelve." Careless, concept, or time?
LEHUA: Pause it and try. Pick the bucket, and say why.
LEHUA: And we're back. Kaden?
KADEN: Careless. Because the setup was right. Point one five times eighty is exactly what you're supposed to do. They just multiplied wrong.
DEREK: Correct. Point one five times eighty is twelve. Ten percent of eighty is eight, five percent is four, eight plus four is twelve. The student knew the method and slipped on the arithmetic. In the app, that trap is called calculation slip.
PONO: Now, what if the student had written eighty divided by fifteen?
KADEN: Then that's concept. They didn't know how percents work.
PONO: And what if they never wrote anything, and just tapped B with three seconds left?
KADEN: Time.
PONO: There you go. Same miss, three different causes, three different fixes.
LEHUA: So what are the fixes?
DEREK: Careless gets a check. Slow down on the last step, and check backward. Twelve divided by eighty is point one five. That's three seconds. Concept gets studied. Open the Strategies tab for that skill, read the steps, and drill ten of that skill. Time gets a pacing fix, which is episode three. Two passes, flag it if you can't see the path in about ten seconds, and keep the checkpoints.
KADEN: So if I mark everything careless, that's bad?
DEREK: If you mark everything careless, you're probably hiding concept misses. Careless feels better. It says, "I'm smart, I just slipped." But if the same skill keeps showing up as careless, it's probably a concept.
PONO: Now here's the part people skip. The redo. The app puts every miss in your error log on the dashboard, with the trap name. Three days later, the item comes back due for a redo. Not the same day. Three days. If you can get it right three days later, you actually learned it. In the app, a skill only counts as Mastered after you get a redo right.
KADEN: Why three days? Why not tomorrow?
PONO: Because tomorrow you still remember the answer. Three days later, you have to remember the method. That's the real test.
LEHUA: And the weekly plan?
DEREK: On the dashboard. You told the app how many minutes a day you have when you set it up. It multiplies by seven and builds your week, weighted toward your weakest skills. It puts a timed module in every week. And if you've entered your test date, it adds a full-length test at fourteen days out and three days out.
LEHUA: And Blitz.
DEREK: Blitz is in Quizzers. Sixty seconds, eight seconds a card, streaks and a high score. It's for the stuff you just have to know cold, like SOH CAH TOA or when to use a semicolon. It's a warm-up, not a study session.
KADEN: I haven't even opened Blitz.
PONO: Then open it this week. A good horse gets better from short rides every day, not one long ride on Sunday.
LEHUA: Recap, Kaden.
KADEN: Every miss goes in one of three buckets. Careless, which is I knew it and slipped. Concept, which is I didn't know the rule. Time, which is I rushed. Be honest about which one. Today's example was fifteen percent of eighty, where they set it up right and got fourteen instead of twelve. That's careless, and the trap is calculation slip. Careless gets a backward check. Concept gets the Strategies tab and a drill. Time gets the two-pass plan. Then redo the miss three days later, because tomorrow I'd just remember the answer. Follow the weekly plan. Blitz is a warm-up.
DEREK: That's the most useful recap you've done. Nine.
KADEN: I'm writing that down in the notebook.
LEHUA: Homework. Open the dashboard and look at your error log. If anything is due, redo it. If nothing is due yet, do a drill of ten, and on every miss, tap the honest button. Then look at your weekly plan and do today's first line.
PONO: And three days from now, come back for the redo. Put it in your phone.
LEHUA: That's episode twelve. Next time, episode thirteen, the last seven days. I gotta go, I have volleyball practice at the district park, and I'm the one with the key to the ball cart.
PONO: Waimea District Park. Hurry up, they waiting.
LEHUA: Thanks for listening, everybody.

sat.title: The Last Seven Days
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode thirteen. I'm Lehua. Coach Pono is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here, and his test is in one week. For real this time.

DEREK: Numbers first, then Coach can do the fun part. English, forty-two seconds a question. Math, sixty-seven. Reading, sixty-seven. Science, if you take it, sixty.
KADEN: Forty-two seconds still sounds fake.
PONO: Forty-two is plenty for most English questions. Most of them are short. One underlined part, four choices. If you know the rule, you're done in fifteen seconds. The trouble is never the easy ones. The trouble is the one question you sit on for three minutes.
LEHUA: Because nobody runs out of time evenly.
PONO: Right. Two or three questions eat the clock, and then the clock tells you about it at the end. So here's the plan. Two passes. Listen, dis part important.
PONO: First pass, go in order. Look at the question. If you can see the path in about ten seconds, do it. If you can't, pick your best guess, mark it, and move on. Online, use the flag. On paper, circle the question number in your test booklet. Don't sit there.

DEREK: And the last sixty seconds, you stop solving. Check that every question has an answer. No blanks. There's no guessing penalty, so a blank is the only answer that's always wrong.
PONO: It's like barrel racing. You go around the barrel, you don't stop to look at it. The one you knocked over, you deal with later.
KADEN: I don't know anything about barrel racing.
PONO: You know enough now.
LEHUA: Okay, checkpoints. Coach, how often should you look at the clock?
PONO: Twice. Not every minute. Twice. At one-third of the time and two-thirds of the time. And you ask one question. Am I at or past the target question?
DEREK: The targets. English, question seventeen at eleven minutes forty, and question thirty-three at twenty-three twenty. Math, question fifteen at sixteen minutes forty, and question thirty at thirty-three twenty. Reading is passages, not questions. Four passages, about ten minutes each, so passage two should be done at twenty minutes.
KADEN: I'm not memorizing all that.
DEREK: You don't have to today. They're on the Time Squeeze page in the app. But here's a nice thing. Those times are minutes used. If you test online, the timer on screen counts down. KADEN: Wait, that's actually clean.
DEREK: Math too. Sixteen forty and thirty-three twenty, both ways.
LEHUA: Let's try one. Kaden, and everybody listening. You're in English. The clock says you've used eleven minutes and forty seconds. You just finished question fourteen. Are you on pace, and what do you do?
LEHUA: Again. English. Eleven forty used. You just finished question fourteen. On pace or not, and what do you do?
PONO: Pause it and try.
PONO: Okay. Kaden.
KADEN: The target at eleven forty is seventeen. I'm on fourteen. So I'm behind by three.
PONO: Behind by three. That's only half of it. The question also asked what you do. Stop at "behind" and the app would call that stopped a step early. So, now what? This is where people panic.
KADEN: Go faster?
PONO: No. Don't read faster. Reading faster makes mistakes. You flag faster. You lower the bar. If a question doesn't show you the path in ten seconds, it gets a guess and a mark, right now, no thinking about it. That's how you catch up. You stop feeding the slow ones.
DEREK: Three questions behind at forty-two seconds each is about two minutes. Flag the next slow one at ten seconds instead of fighting it for two minutes, and you've made most of that back.
KADEN: And if I'm ahead?
PONO: Slow down one notch. Ahead is fine. Ahead and careless is the problem. Use the extra seconds to read every word of the question.
LEHUA: The app does this for you, right?
DEREK: In Timed, it checks you at one-third and two-thirds. It'll say on pace, or it'll say behind pace, flag the long ones and move. Same words Coach just said.
PONO: The app stole my line.
DEREK: You stole it first.
KADEN: Okay, what about Reading? That's where I die.
PONO: Reading is ten minutes a passage. No exceptions. If a passage is eating you alive at minute nine, you answer what's left with your best guesses and you go to the next passage. The next passage might be your best one. Don't let a bad one steal the time from a good one.
KADEN: That's like my cousin's car. The gas light comes on and he says it's fine for another twenty miles. It's never fine.
LEHUA: So the gas light is your checkpoint.
KADEN: The gas light is my checkpoint. Okay, I get it.

LEHUA: Kaden, recap. Your words.

DEREK: You got the mirror trick. That was the best part. Seven.

act.title: Where the Sentence Breaks, ACT Edition
act.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to ACT Notes, episode four. I'm Lehua. Sarah is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here, and I think his eyes finished loading.
KADEN: Ninety percent. Still buffering a little.
SARAH: That's progress.
LEHUA: Warm-up from last time. Kaden, ACT English. What question should you be on at eleven minutes forty?
KADEN: Seventeen. And if I'm behind, I flag faster, not read faster.
LEHUA: Good. So how do you get through English questions fast enough to make seventeen? You know the rules cold. Today is a rule that shows up all over the English section. Where the sentence breaks. Sarah, you've been waiting all week.
SARAH: I have. My mom texted me this morning. "I'm at the store, I'll be home soon."
KADEN: That's a normal text.
SARAH: It's a comma splice. Two complete sentences glued together with only a comma. I texted back a semicolon.
LEHUA: Just the semicolon?
SARAH: Just the semicolon. She knows what it means.
DEREK: Does she?
SARAH: She does now.
LEHUA: Okay, teach it. Why does punctuation matter so much on ACT English?
SARAH: Because punctuation questions show up again and again, and they're some of the most learnable points on the whole test. There are only a few rules. Once you know them, these questions take you ten seconds.
SARAH: Here's the move. The app calls it "what's on each side." Find the punctuation mark being tested. Then look left of it and right of it, and label each side. Is it a full sentence that could stand alone? Or is it just a piece, a phrase?
KADEN: How do I know if it's a full sentence?
SARAH: It has a subject and a verb, and it makes sense if you put a period after it. "The tide was low." Full sentence. "When the tide was low." Not a full sentence. That word "when" makes it wait for something.
SARAH: Now the rule. If both sides are full sentences, you have three options. A period. A semicolon. Or a comma plus a joining word like and, but, or so. That's it. A comma by itself is not allowed. That's the comma splice my mom did.
DEREK: So a semicolon is basically a period that doesn't end the sentence.
SARAH: Between two full sentences, yes. Exactly that.
SARAH: And two more marks. A colon and a dash. On the ACT, the safe rule is that the part before a colon has to be a full sentence. The colon says, here comes the thing I promised. Same for a dash when it's setting something up.
KADEN: Like a semicolon is a save point. The level ends, but you keep going.
SARAH: I will allow that.
LEHUA: Okay. Let's do one. Sarah, read it.
SARAH: I'll read the sentence, then the four choices. Listen for where the sentence breaks. "The tide was low, we walked out to the reef." The underlined part is "low, we." Choices. A, No Change, so low comma we. B, low semicolon we. C, low we, with no punctuation at all. D, low semicolon and we.
SARAH: One more time. "The tide was low, we walked out to the reef." A, low comma we. B, low semicolon we. C, low we, nothing. D, low semicolon and we.
LEHUA: Pause it and try. Label each side first.
LEHUA: Okay, we're back. Kaden.
KADEN: Left side, "The tide was low." That's a full sentence. Right side, "we walked out to the reef." Also full. So both sides are full sentences.
SARAH: Good. That's the whole question right there. Now which choices are allowed for two full sentences?
KADEN: Period, semicolon, or comma plus and. So B, the semicolon.
SARAH: B. Let's kill the others, because the wrong ones are the lesson. C has nothing between two full sentences. That's a run-on. Cross it out. D has a semicolon and the word and together. You use one or the other, not both. Cross it out.
SARAH: And A. A is the trap we're naming today. The app calls it near miss. It looks almost right. It's one tiny mark away from correct. If it said comma and, it would be fine. With just the comma, it's a comma splice. And it's the one people pick because it sounds right when you say it out loud.
KADEN: Because you pause there.
SARAH: Because you pause there. That's the other trap the app warns you about: adding commas wherever you would pause when you're talking. Your voice is not a punctuation rule. Label the sides instead.
DEREK: Also, notice that A was No Change. On the ACT, No Change is right sometimes. Not always, not never. Don't avoid it, and don't fall in love with it. Test it like any other choice.
LEHUA: Okay, Sarah, one more piece. Apostrophes, quick.
SARAH: Quick. Ask two questions. Does something own something? And how many owners? One student's notebook, apostrophe before the s. Two students' notebooks, apostrophe after the s. And "its" with no apostrophe means belonging to it. "It's" with an apostrophe means it is. Say "it is" in the sentence. If that works, use the apostrophe.
KADEN: That's the one I always mess up.
SARAH: Everybody does. That's why it's on the test.
LEHUA: And in the app, when you miss one of these, you'll see that label. Trap, near miss. So you'll know it was almost right, and you can find the one tiny mark that broke it.
DEREK: Then it goes in your error log, and you redo it in three days.
LEHUA: Kaden, recap. Your words.
KADEN: Find the mark, then label both sides. Full sentence or just a piece. Two full sentences get a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus and, but, or so. Comma alone is a comma splice. A colon needs a full sentence before it. No Change is sometimes right, so test it. The trap was near miss, like the comma that's one word away from right. Don't put commas where you pause. Its with no apostrophe means belonging to it.
DEREK: That was every rule, in order, with the trap. Eight.
KADEN: Eight. Up from last week.
DEREK: Don't get comfortable.
LEHUA: Homework. Open the app, go to Drill, and pick the punctuation skill. Before every answer, say both labels in your head, full or piece, then pick the mark. When you miss one, read the trap label.
LEHUA: That's episode four. Next time is episode five, Shorter Is Usually Right. Thanks for listening, everybody. I gotta run. Somebody told me there's one slice of chocolate cake left at the barbecue place on the main road.
KADEN: Who told you that?
LEHUA: Nobody. But if I leave now, it's true.

act.title: Shorter Is Usually Right
act.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to ACT Notes, episode five. I'm Lehua. Sarah is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here and already eating.
KADEN: It's a musubi. It's brain food.
SARAH: It's rice food.
LEHUA: Warm-up from last time. Kaden, two full sentences. What can you put between them?
KADEN: A period, a semicolon, or a comma plus and, but, or so. Comma alone is a comma splice.
SARAH: Perfect.
LEHUA: Good. Today is the rest of grammar. Sarah, the title of this episode is "Shorter Is Usually Right." Is that true?
SARAH: Usually. On ACT English, when two choices say the same thing and both are correct, the shorter one tends to win. Extra words that repeat an idea are wrong on this test. But notice the word usually. Shorter loses when it breaks a rule. So today is two rules, and then the shortcut.
SARAH: Rule one. Strip to the core. Find the subject and the verb, and cross out everything between them. Listen. "The box of old records are on the shelf." Sounds kind of okay, right?
KADEN: Kind of.
SARAH: Cross out "of old records." Now it's "The box are on the shelf."
KADEN: Oh, that's bad. The box is.
SARAH: The box is. The verb matches the box, not the records. The app warns you about this exact trap: matching the verb to a nearby noun instead of the real subject. The test often puts a plural noun right next to the verb to pull you in.
SARAH: Same idea for pronouns. A pronoun has to match the noun it stands for in number. "The team lost its first game." The team is one team, so on the ACT it's its, not their.
SARAH: And tense. Keep the verbs in the same time as the rest of the passage. If the paragraph is in the past, a random present-tense verb is probably the wrong answer.
LEHUA: Rule two. Modifiers.
SARAH: A modifier is a describing phrase. The rule is that it has to sit right next to the thing it describes. When that thing is in the wrong spot, it's a misplaced modifier. When it's missing from the sentence completely, it's a dangling modifier. Either way, the sentence says something ridiculous.
LEHUA: Let's do one. Read it twice.
SARAH: "Driving up the hill, the fog made the road hard to see." Which version is correct? A, No Change. B, "Driving up the hill, we could barely see the road through the fog." C, "While driving up the hill, the fog made the road hard to see." D, "Driving up the hill, the road was hard to see in the fog."
SARAH: Again. "Driving up the hill, the fog made the road hard to see." A, No Change. B, "Driving up the hill, we could barely see the road through the fog." C, "While driving up the hill, the fog made the road hard to see." D, "Driving up the hill, the road was hard to see in the fog."
LEHUA: Pause it and try. Ask who's driving.
LEHUA: Okay, we're back. Kaden, who's driving?
KADEN: In A, the fog. The fog is driving up the hill. Which, okay, that's kind of how it feels in my uncle's truck, but no.
SARAH: Right. The phrase "driving up the hill" attaches to whatever comes right after the comma. In A, that's the fog. Cross it out. D?
KADEN: D, the road is driving. Also no.
SARAH: Cross it out. Now C. C is the trap we're naming today. Near miss. It changed one thing. It added "while." It looks like somebody fixed it. But the next word is still "the fog," so the fog is still driving. One small change, still broken.
KADEN: So B. "We" are driving.
SARAH: B. The people are right after the comma, so the people are driving. And here's the twist. B is the longest choice.
KADEN: So the title is lying.
SARAH: The title says usually. Shorter wins only among the choices that are correct. Grammar first, then length. Rule, then shortcut.
DEREK: That's the same as math. The shortcut only counts if the answer is right.
LEHUA: Okay, now the shortcut itself.
SARAH: Redundancy. Saying the same thing twice. "In my opinion, I think the plan is good." "In my opinion" and "I think" are the same idea. Cut one. "The hotel was built recently, a few months ago." Recently and a few months ago, same idea. Cut one.
SARAH: And sometimes one of the choices is OMIT. That means delete the underlined part completely. When the sentence still makes sense and keeps its meaning without those words, OMIT is often right. So the habit is to check OMIT or the shortest choice first. If it keeps the meaning and it's grammatical, take it.
KADEN: So OMIT is like the skip button.
SARAH: OMIT is the skip button, but only when you lose nothing by skipping.
DEREK: And don't pick it because it's short. Read the sentence without the words. If it still says the same thing, good. If the meaning changes, it's wrong.
LEHUA: Sarah, how fast should these go?
SARAH: Fast. Grammar questions are where you bank time for the harder ones. Strip to the core, check the modifier, check the shortest. That's maybe fifteen seconds when you know the rules. That buys you time for the questions about what a paragraph is trying to do. That's next week.
LEHUA: And in the app, when you miss one, you'll see the label "Trap, near miss." That's your hint that the choice you picked fixed something, just not the real problem.
DEREK: Then find the one word that broke it, and redo the question when the error log says it's due. That's what the redo in three days is for.
LEHUA: Kaden, recap. Your words.
KADEN: Two rules and a shortcut. One, strip to the core. Cross out the stuff between the subject and the verb, then match them. Same with pronouns, and keep the tense the same. Two, the describing phrase has to sit next to what it describes, so ask who's doing it. Then the shortcut. Don't say the same thing twice. Check OMIT or the shortest choice first, but only if it's still correct. Grammar first, then shorter. The trap was near miss, like adding "while" and the fog is still driving.
DEREK: The fog is still driving. You'll remember that. Eight.
KADEN: The fog is still driving. That's going on a shirt.
LEHUA: Homework. Open the app, go to Drill, and pick grammar and usage. On every question, do the strip. Cross out the middle in your head and match the subject and verb. Then check the Strategies tab for the four steps if you get stuck.
LEHUA: That's episode five. Next time is episode six, What Is This Sentence For. Thanks for listening, everybody. I'm going to bed early. Saturday morning hike up to the pond.
KADEN: How early?
LEHUA: Early enough that the fog is still driving.

act.title: What Is This Sentence For?
act.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to ACT Notes, episode six. I'm Lehua. Sarah is here, Derek is here, and Kaden made it with zero minutes to spare.
KADEN: The bus driver waved at me like he knew. He knew.
LEHUA: Warm-up from last time. Kaden, a describing phrase at the start of a sentence. What's the rule?
KADEN: It has to sit right next to the thing it describes. Otherwise the fog is driving.
SARAH: The fog is driving forever now.
LEHUA: Good. Last week was rules. This week, there's no rule to memorize. Sarah, what are these questions?
SARAH: These are the questions where the ACT asks you to think like the writer. The question isn't "is this grammatical?" It's "what is this sentence for?" There are a few kinds. Some ask which choice best accomplishes a goal. Some ask whether the writer should add a sentence or delete it. Some ask which transition fits, and sometimes they ask where a sentence should go.
KADEN: Those are the ones where every answer is grammatically fine and I just pick a vibe.
SARAH: Exactly. And that's why people miss them. Every choice is a fine sentence. The question is which one does the job. So the first move is to read the question and find the job. The goal is written right there in the question. Most people skip past it to get to the choices.
LEHUA: Let's do one now, so we can talk about it.
SARAH: Here's the setup. A paragraph about a canoe club. Then the question. "The writer wants to show that the club welcomes beginners. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?" A, "The club was started more than forty years ago." B, "New paddlers can join any practice, and coaches pair them with experienced paddlers." C, "The club's canoes are heavy and hard to carry." D, "The club races most weekends in the summer."
SARAH: One more time. The goal is, show that the club welcomes beginners. A, "The club was started more than forty years ago." B, "New paddlers can join any practice, and coaches pair them with experienced paddlers." C, "The club's canoes are heavy and hard to carry." D, "The club races most weekends in the summer."
LEHUA: Pause it and try. Say the goal back first.
LEHUA: Okay, we're back. Kaden.
KADEN: The goal is beginners are welcome. So B. New paddlers, and coaches help them.
SARAH: B. Now let's look at the wrong ones, because that's where the lesson is. C. Heavy canoes. Does that show beginners are welcome?
KADEN: It kind of does the opposite. It sounds hard.
SARAH: Cross it out. D. Races most summer weekends. Maybe true, but nothing about beginners. Cross it out. And A. Started forty years ago. Same problem as D, and it's the trap we're naming today. The app calls it true but irrelevant.
KADEN: But it could be true.
SARAH: It could be totally true. It could be in the paragraph already. It might even be interesting. But the question asked for one job, welcoming beginners, and A doesn't do that job. True but irrelevant is one of the most tempting wrong answers on these questions, because it's real information. It just answers a question nobody asked.
DEREK: In math terms, it's a correct number for the wrong question.
SARAH: That's a good way to say it.
LEHUA: Okay, add or delete. Sarah.
SARAH: The question says something like, "The writer is considering deleting this sentence. Should the writer make this deletion?" And the choices are two yeses and two nos, each with a reason. Here's the test the app uses. Would the paragraph lose anything if this sentence vanished? If it would lose something it needs, keep it. If nothing is lost, delete it.
SARAH: And here's the part people miss. Getting yes or no right is only half the question. You still have to pick the right reason. The app warns you about exactly this trap: choosing yes or no correctly but picking the wrong reason. So decide yes or no, then read both reasons on your side and pick the one that matches what the sentence actually does.
KADEN: So it's like getting the right answer on a math problem but showing the wrong work.
SARAH: On the ACT, the wrong work costs you the point.
LEHUA: Last piece. Transitions.
SARAH: Read the sentence before the transition and the sentence after. Then name the link in one word. Contrast, like however. Cause, like therefore. Addition, like also. Or order, like then. The right transition has to fit both neighbors, not just the one after it.
SARAH: Quick one. "The trail was steep. Blank, the view at the top was worth it." What's the link?
KADEN: Steep is bad, view is good. So contrast. However.
SARAH: However. Not therefore. The steep trail didn't cause the good view.
DEREK: And if a question asks where a sentence should go, look for a word that points back. "This," "that," "these," "also." It has to come after the thing it's pointing at.
KADEN: So if a sentence starts with "these problems," the problems have to show up before it.
DEREK: Right. You can't point at something nobody has mentioned yet.
LEHUA: How long should these take, Sarah? They feel slower than grammar.
SARAH: They are a little slower. That's okay. You banked time on the grammar ones. The app's suggested time for these is about fifty seconds. Just don't reread the whole passage. Reread the paragraph around the sentence. That's enough.
LEHUA: Kaden, recap. Your words.
KADEN: These are "what is this sentence for" questions. Read the question first and say the goal back. Pick the choice that does that job. The trap is true but irrelevant, like the club being forty years old. It's true, it's just not the job. For add or delete, ask if the paragraph loses anything, then pick yes or no and also the right reason. For transitions, name the link and make it fit both sentences.
DEREK: You named the trap with an example. That's how you'll spot it. Nine.
KADEN: Nine? What happened?
DEREK: You happened.
LEHUA: Homework. Open the app, go to Drill, and pick topic development. Before you look at the choices, say the writer's goal out loud. When you miss one, read the label. If it says true but irrelevant, ask what job the question wanted.
LEHUA: That's episode six. Next time is episode seven, Backsolve, Plug In, Move On. That's math. Thanks for listening, everybody. I gotta go, I have volleyball practice at the district park.
KADEN: You play volleyball?
LEHUA: I play the part of a person who plays volleyball. Bye.

act.title: Backsolve, Plug In, Move On
act.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to ACT Notes, episode seven. I'm Lehua. We're doing math today, so Derek is here, Coach Pono is here, and Kaden is here with a calculator he says he's had since sixth grade.
KADEN: It's been through things. It still works.
DEREK: Check the ACT calculator policy before test day. Make sure it's allowed.
KADEN: It's a regular calculator.
DEREK: Then it's probably fine. Check anyway. And if you test online, there's a graphing calculator built into the screen.
LEHUA: Warm-up from last time. Kaden, what does true but irrelevant mean?
KADEN: The choice is true, and it might even be in the passage, but it doesn't do the job the question asked for. Like the canoe club being forty years old.
LEHUA: Good. Okay, math. Derek, the title is three verbs. Backsolve, plug in, move on.
DEREK: Three tools. Here's the idea behind all three. On a multiple-choice math test, the answer is already on the screen. One of those four choices is right. Sometimes the fastest way to find it is to stop doing algebra and start testing the choices.
KADEN: Wait, that's allowed?
DEREK: It's not cheating. It's reading the test. And you have a calculator for the whole ACT math section, so testing a number takes seconds.
DEREK: Tool one. Backsolve. Use it when the choices are numbers and the question asks for one value. Start with a middle choice, test it in the problem, and see if it's too big or too small. Then move the right way. Let's do one.
DEREK: Student tickets to a game cost five dollars. Adult tickets cost eight dollars. A group of twelve people paid seventy-five dollars total. How many adults were in the group? A, three. B, four. C, five. D, seven.
DEREK: Once more. Students five dollars, adults eight dollars. Twelve people, seventy-five dollars total. How many adults? A, three. B, four. C, five. D, seven.
LEHUA: Pause it and try. Start with a middle choice.
LEHUA: Okay, we're back. Kaden.
KADEN: I'll start with B, four adults. Four times eight is thirty-two. That leaves eight students, eight times five is forty. Thirty-two plus forty is seventy-two.
DEREK: Seventy-two. Is that the total?
KADEN: No, it's seventy-five. So I'm three short.
DEREK: Which way do you move?

act.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to ACT Notes, episode eight. I'm Lehua. It's a math one, so it's me, Derek, and Kaden, who brought graph paper for some reason.
KADEN: You said grid. I brought a grid.

LEHUA: Warm-up from last time. Kaden, when you backsolve, where do you start?
KADEN: A middle choice. Test it, then go up or down. And write down what the question wants before I start.
LEHUA: Good. Today is functions and graphs. Derek, a lot of people freeze the second they see f of x.
DEREK: They do. So let's take the scary part out. F of x is a machine. You put in a number, it gives you a number. The number you put in is x. The number you get out is f of x. That's it.
DEREK: On a graph, x goes across. The output goes up. So f of five means: go across to five, then go up or down until you hit the graph, and read how high you are. F of five is a height. A y-value.
KADEN: So f of five isn't five.
DEREK: F of five usually isn't five. Five is what you put in. F of five is what comes out.
LEHUA: Let's do one. Derek, read it twice.
DEREK: Picture a grid. The graph of f is a straight line. It goes through the point zero comma three, and the point two comma seven. What is f of five? A, two. B, five. C, ten. D, thirteen.
DEREK: One more time. A straight line through zero comma three, and two comma seven. What is f of five? A, two. B, five. C, ten. D, thirteen.
LEHUA: Pause it and try. You can sketch it if you want.
LEHUA: Okay, we're back. Kaden, you have actual graph paper.
KADEN: Okay. Zero, three, that's on the up-and-down axis, three up. Then two, seven. So from x equals zero to x equals two, it went up from three to seven. That's up four.
DEREK: Up four, over how many?
KADEN: Over two. So the slope is four over two. Two.
DEREK: Slope first. The app's tip for this whole skill is "slope first, most coordinate questions are slope in disguise." Keep going.
KADEN: So it starts at three and goes up two every step. The equation is f of x equals two x plus three. F of five is two times five, ten, plus three. Thirteen. D.
DEREK: D, thirteen. Now the wrong ones. B is five. That's the input. We just talked about that. C is ten. That's two times five without the starting value. You did part of the work and forgot the three. And A. A is two.
KADEN: That's the slope.
DEREK: That's the slope. And that's the trap we're naming today. The app calls it answers the wrong part. Two is a real number from this problem. You found it. You needed it. But the question asked for f of five, not the slope. The test loves to put a number you computed along the way into the choices.
KADEN: Because when I see a number I just got, I'm like, oh, that's mine.
DEREK: Exactly. It feels familiar, so you grab it. So before you pick, reread the last line of the question. What did they ask for? A slope? A y-value? An x-value? Match that.
LEHUA: Okay, quadratics. Derek, short version.
DEREK: Short version. A quadratic makes a U shape, or an upside-down U. The app's tip is, use the form that shows what they ask for. If they ask where the graph crosses the x-axis, you want factored form. Y equals x minus two, times x minus six. It crosses at two and at six. Flip the signs.
DEREK: If they ask for the highest point or the lowest point, you want vertex form. Y equals negative, x minus three squared, plus seven. The highest point is seven, and it happens at x equals three. The number at the end is the height.
KADEN: So again, they could ask for the three or the seven.
DEREK: They could ask for either one. Same trap. If they ask for the maximum value, that's seven. If they ask where the maximum happens, that's three. Answer the part they asked.
LEHUA: And calculators. You can use one on every ACT math question. So why not just use it for everything?
DEREK: Because typing is slower than seeing. Calculator discipline. Use it for arithmetic you'd get wrong in your head, like big multiplication or decimals. Use it to check. Don't use it to avoid thinking. In the example we just did, nothing needed a calculator. Up four, over two, slope two. If you'd typed all that in, you'd have spent more time and learned nothing.
KADEN: So calculator for the boss fight, not the tutorial.
DEREK: That's a good line. Also, know your calculator before test day. If you test online, there's a graphing calculator built into the screen, so practice with it, or bring the one you know. If you're fumbling for the minus key on the real test, that's a pace problem.
LEHUA: Derek, when should someone flag one of these and move on?
DEREK: Same rule as always. Ten seconds, can you see the path? On graph questions the path is usually, find the slope or find the form. If you can't tell what kind of function it is, guess, flag, and come back.
LEHUA: Kaden, recap. Your words.
KADEN: F of x is a machine. X goes in, f of x comes out. F of five is the height of the graph at five, not five. Slope first. How far it goes up, over how far it goes across. Factored form gives you where it crosses, vertex form gives you the highest or lowest point. Calculator for arithmetic and checking, not for stuff I can see. The trap was answers the wrong part, like picking the slope when they asked for f of five. Reread the last line before I pick.
DEREK: Up over across. That's slope in one sentence. Eight.
KADEN: That's going on a shirt too.
DEREK: You're going to need more shirts.
LEHUA: Homework. Open the app, go to Drill, and pick coordinate geometry. On every graph question, find the slope first, and before you tap a choice, say what the question asked for. Slope, x, or y.
